item.title: When Our Partner Won't Take Responsibility for Hurting Us
item.description:
Relationships

When Our Partner Won't Take Responsibility for Hurting Us

We can't change our defensive partner, but we can change our response.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • As women, our instinct is to keep trying to make things better until we run out of steam.
  • We must recognize that we cannot change our partner if they don’t want to change.
  • The loss of connection with our partner feels terrifying and dangerous.

This post is Part 1 of a series.

In relationships, we get hurt by our partner. It’s unavoidable. Usually the wounding is unintentional, but it happens. The worst pain we experience usually comes not from the original hurt but from the response we receive when sharing our hurt.

The Cycle of Sharing Hurt and Receiving Emotional Attack

Have you ever had the experience of telling your partner about something they did that upset you and no matter how clearly, lovingly, non-blamingly you express your hurt, somehow you end up getting emotionally attacked? Have you ever tried to express feeling victimized, even if it was unintentional, only to become the perpetrator in your partner’s story? That suddenly you’ve become responsible for hurting them and accusing them of doing something wrong, suggesting that they’ve done something they never did, or if they did do it, then it shouldn’t have hurt you? But your pain is completely ignored; it’s all about the “accusation.” In a split second, you’ve gone from being the one hurting and needing to be heard, to being the aggressor who’s attacking them. Sharing your upset, which began as an attempt to create closeness and change a situation that wasn’t working for you, creates more conflict and more distance. Instead of empathy and understanding, or the unthinkable—an apology—you receive anger, irrationality, and rejection. In a flash, what was a bid for empathy and connection has devolved into a severe rupture and a charged emotional battle. What you’d hoped would create an emotional or physical hug has catapulted you into a struggle for survival, both for yourself and the relationship.

If you’re someone who has lived this experience many times, it can be hard to know how to move the dial forward and make things better in the relationship, to convey what doesn’t work for you. While you want to make your partner aware of the ways they hurt you, probably unintentionally, so that they can stop or change the behaviors, it seems that it’s not possible, not without ending up in a huge fight or being attacked emotionally. So, what then?

For this post, I’m going to assume that you’ve already tried to explain this pattern to your partner, probably many times, and to point out that it’s not that they intended to hurt you but that they did hurt you—and this matters. Perhaps you’ve drawn the analogy of stepping on someone’s toe (or something similar), and that while the person didn’t mean to do it, it still hurt, and most people still apologize. Or perhaps you’ve shared that the mere fact that your partner’s behavior upsets you—someone they presumably love—that this should be enough of a reason to want to change it. You’ve probably pointed out (multiple times) that there’s no blame, and it’s not about your partner’s failing or inadequacy but about having your experience acknowledged and cared for. My guess is that you’ve tried many different approaches to making the situation better, to get what you need and in the long run make the bond tighter and more connected. But what if none of that works, which it often doesn’t?

As women, our instinct is to keep trying to make things better until we literally run out of steam, to keep explaining a situation that’s hurting us in a thousand different ways. We imagine that our partner will have to get it sooner or later, that we haven’t said it just right yet or at the right time or with the right intonation. We hold onto the hope (fantasy?) that they will understand that our hurt matters and is not about them but rather—about us. And then they will hear us, acknowledge our pain, know us, and want to change. Then, when they get it, we’ll be able to exhale and relax. But often, they don’t get it and never move beyond what our hurt says about them; they never make the shift from about them to about us, the defenses never relent. They don’t apologize but continue to blame us for the experience they think we’re blaming on them. Again and again, when we share, we end up more hurt, more wounded, and more attacked—even lonelier than before we opened our mouth.

Accepting That We Can't Change Another Person

As we know, we cannot change another person. The only person we can change is ourselves. It’s a fairly easy thing to understand intellectually, but not remotely easy to accept in our heart and body. This conversation is not designed to blame ourselves even more; we’ve got enough of that if we’re with a blaming and defensive partner. But it is about recognizing where we may be contributing to a dysfunctional system, and repeating a pattern that enables it to continue. As much as I’ve always hated the question (because it suggests that something else is our fault), still, we must ask ourselves, What part am I playing in all this; how am I enabling this system to go on?

The question involves recognizing (and accepting?) that we cannot change our partner if they don’t want to change. Of this we have to be certain, and remind ourselves that we’ve already tried and tried, and tried. We’ve tried, and the results are the same; no matter how clear, concise, well-timed, and skillful our explanation, or how we reframe the problem, we’re not going to receive the empathy we so deeply crave. We’re not going to get the relief in knowing that our experience matters simply because it’s our experience. And certainly, we’re not going to get the apology we want. None of it is going to happen. Our partner’s insecurity, shame, sense of inadequacy, or whatever else stands in the way of their being able to acknowledge our hurt and own their part in it is too daunting and dangerous to get near.

In Part 2 of this series, I’ll describe the most prevalent pattern I see women repeating, the part we play that enables this defensive, unkind, and deeply unsatisfying system to go on, keeping us frustrated, sad, and stuck in our own relational Groundhog Day.

Before going any further, however, I want to first insist that we approach any self-inquiry with profound and fierce self-compassion. We must start with the understanding that when it comes to these situations, we’re often in a state of fight or flight, operating from our deepest and most primal drive—our survival instinct. We play out the pattern I will describe in Part 2—not because it moves the dial forward for us or the relationship, and definitely not because it feels good, but because we desperately need to preserve the connection with our partner, to get back to OK, keep the peace, and return to the status quo, no matter what the cost. It feels like life and death. The loss of connection with our partner feels terrifying and dangerous, like we literally won’t be able to survive it, no matter how strong we are. At the same time, our drive to protect our children, if there are children in the mix, is deeply wired into us and keeps us locked in a cycle in which we’ll do anything to restore calm in the home. The overriding sentiment is that we must hold onto the connection and get back to OK, no matter what, even if it means abandoning ourselves.

item.title: What Makes a Laughter Theory Comprehensive?
item.description:
Laughter

What Makes a Laughter Theory Comprehensive?

A full account of laughter and humor must address these common topics.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • This blog has taken in-depth looks at numerous subjects relating to laughter and humor.
  • The big-picture view should consider what a comprehensive theory of laughter must able to explain.
  • Scholars attempting to understand this enigmatic behavior often address nine common topics.

This blog has examined laughter and humor from a variety of perspectives, usually by taking a deep dive into specific examples. I’ve analyzed the work of various comedians and pranksters, deconstructed television comedies and their characters, assessed general comedic themes, considered laughter’s relationship to play and tickling behavior, evaluated variations in our laugh response, and addressed many other topics. I’ve also made repeated reference to my own explanatory account, the Mutual Vulnerability Theory of Laughter, and suggested it’s the most comprehensive theory available.

Source: Josiah Matthew / Pexels

I’d like to take a few minutes to reflect on how I came to make such a bold assertion. After all, over the centuries, numerous thinkers developed dozens of laughter and humor theories I could have chosen from (Amir, 2024). How did I conclude that existing accounts, even when used in combination, were not up to the task, and the one I developed was broad enough and illuminating enough to reliably do the job?

In this post, I want to set aside the micro lens I typically employ and offer up a bird's-eye view of laughter and humor theory. Exactly how might one determine whether any theory is suitably comprehensive to truly explain why we produce this rather odd vocalization?

Seeking the questions

Here, I’m going to rely on a review article I wrote for the European Journal of Humour Research titled "Essential Attributes of a Comprehensive Theory of Laughter" (Simon, 2020), in which I summarized the results of an extensive search for the topics scholars raised in various peer-reviewed articles. I did this by searching numerous journal catalogues, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar for papers containing “laugh,” “laughed,” “laughter,” or “laughing” in the title or subtitle. The resulting list contained 525 articles or reports published in 345 different scientific and medical journals. The various topics the authors addressed were then divided into 29 broad themes. The variety of subject matter will give you a sense of just how difficult it is to construct a single theory capable of answering all the questions raised with respect to laughter and its first cousin, humor.

Theme party

Some of the more common themes originating from my search were as follows.

Physiological. Because many of the articles found were in medical journals, it’s no surprise that the most often raised subject matter related to atypical laughing behavior, specifically the effects of cognitive or emotional disability or injury on one’s expression of laughter and feelings (or lack thereof) of amusement. This would include the symptoms and causes of conditions such as gelastic epilepsy and pseudobulbar affect.

Source: Marko Tuokko / Pexels

Social. Laughter and humor clearly have numerous effects on our lives. This theme delves into their social influences, group dynamics, and the transfer of information, for example, how humor helps prompt informal play, facilitates formal education, or influences people’s belief systems generally.

Brain. For neuroscientists, including those who investigate atypical laughter, understanding where in the brain the stimulus for laughter originates is paramount. Like the physiological theme, this is less about why we laugh and more about how. As such, it tends not to be of great import to scholars theorizing about the functional role laughter plays in our lives.

Physical Benefits. Many have claimed that the expression of laughter itself has a positive effect on our physical well-being, and researchers seek to understand if this is, indeed, the case. Those who practice laughter yoga are among those interested.

Coping. Laughter, and presumably the humor that often inspires it, seems to bolster our ability to weather emotional turmoil, including feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and mild depression.

Variation. Subject matter relating to variations in the laugh responses was incredibly diverse, but, to be at all manageable, was lumped together under this single heading. Variations included factors such as age, personal history, social context, sex, and health, among dozens of others.

Humor. It’s been obvious for millennia that there is a connection between laughter and humor, but understanding how one relates causally to the other has been exceedingly difficult to pin down. Can something be humorous even if no one responds with laughter?

Function. Scholars interested in human behavior in general would naturally ask why laughter evolved in the first place. What is its function? How might it provide a competitive advantage to those who employ it?

Source: Alexander Krivitskiy / Pexels

Misinterpretation. Whether laughter conveys a message or not, there seem to be times when one’s laughter is taken the wrong way. Typically, this manifests when the laughter one intends to be sympathetic and supportive is instead interpreted by others as being mean-spirited. The potential impact on the relationship bond can be significant and fascinates many psychologists, sociologists, and therapists.

The laughter and humor landscape

This is only a partial list, but one can begin to appreciate how complex the subjects of laughter and humor really are and how wide-ranging and versatile any theory constructed to explain them must be. We laugh at all manner of things, for all sorts of reasons, and its expression has important, sometimes long-lasting effects on our emotional state, as well as that of others nearby. The concept of humor, especially, is notoriously difficult to define. It can be assessed quite differently depending on one’s age, personal background, and cultural heritage, for example. A fully comprehensive laughter theory must be able to stretch, twist, and bend as needed, but not break from its central tenets.

I’ll return with further examples of relevant topics in upcoming posts. For now, you can begin to appreciate just how daunting a task it is to compose a single explanation for laughter capable of explaining its innumerable qualities and motivations.

item.title: DBT for All: Making Mental Health Skills More Accessible
item.description:
Self-Help

DBT for All: Making Mental Health Skills More Accessible

An interview with Shireen Rizvi and Jesse Finkelstein on how their book can help.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • The new book "Real Skills for Real Life" seeks to make evidence-based DBT skills more accessible.
  • DBT skills can help with various mental health difficulties, but self-help resources are still limited.
  • Illustrations and flowcharts can help make complex therapeutic processes more concrete, fun, or flexible.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is an evidence-based psychotherapy that can help people manage intense emotions, build better relationships, and cope with the stressors of today’s world, in part by teaching dozens of coping skills.

Research shows that learning the DBT skills alone can help people improve their mental health in various ways,1 but there aren’t enough DBT therapists to go around, and more self-help resources are needed.

Two DBT experts, Drs. Jesse Finkelstein and Shireen Rizvi, have spent years working to close that gap. Their new, fully illustrated book, Real Skills for Real Life, teaches DBT skills in a simple, fun, and unique way. I sat down with them to talk about what it takes to make DBT's skills feel truly accessible. No therapist required.

Kiki Fehling: Let’s start with the basics: Why did the two of you want to write this book?

Jesse Finkelstein: DBT is built around a skills-deficit model: the idea that what often keeps someone from living a life worth living is that they don't yet have skills to help them move toward their goals. And, as DBT clinicians, we don't just teach these skills; we use them ourselves! We believe these are skills for living that everyone deserves access to.

Shireen Rizvi: Right, we wanted more people to have access to these skills, but we particularly wanted to do it in a user-friendly way so that more people would want to learn the skills. The official DBT skills manual is amazing. It's been found to be effective. And it's a bit intimidating. So part of our mission was to create a self-help book that would help readers with different backgrounds, learning styles, and interests.

KF: I assume that focus on accessibility is why the book leans so heavily on images and pictures—they’re all so fabulous! What drew you in that direction?

JF: The collaboration between us actually started with the DBT skills videos Shireen's lab produced during COVID—short animated videos teaching individual skills. As of today, those have around 4 million views. Given how popular and accessible that pairing of DBT skills with fun illustrations turned out to be, we were inspired to think, OK, how could we do that in a book format?

KF: I also love the flowcharts at the start of the book. As a DBT teacher, I often hear: "DBT has so many skills; how do I figure out which one to use when?" Your flowcharts offer an answer to this hard question. How did you come up with them?

JF: We asked: What's the true organizing principle for how people might use the book? In a moment of strong emotion, no one is going to remember “turn to page 36!” We tried to build the flowcharts around common themes of experiences—"I'm in a crisis” or "I'm ruminating"—that people might recognize.

KF: Organizing the flowcharts around lived experience, rather than the DBT modules, offers something different from many other DBT self-help books. It captures something a therapist does that is actually quite complex!

SR: A flowchart can do something else a therapist would: help people see the diversity of skills available. People often learn one skill, and then they apply it to every situation without realizing that maybe it isn’t actually the most effective skill here. The flowchart offers options, so people get to try something outside their comfort zone.

KF: Did iterating the flowcharts or writing this book change how you understand or teach DBT skills?

JF: Check The Facts was something we really wrestled with. How do you concisely explain to someone who doesn’t have a therapist what you’re actually supposed to do with that skill?

SR: In the DBT manual, Check The Facts is a list of questions to ask yourself about a situation, but it doesn't say much about what to do with the answers to those questions. A skilled therapist can take that and build on it in the room. On the page, we needed something more concrete and standalone, since there wasn't going to be a therapist there to fill in that gap.

JF: The Model of Emotions is a good example of that same challenge. It's a brilliant way of conceptualizing emotion, but it isn't always easy or appealing for someone to do on their own without a therapist. We wanted this book to feel friendly and fun and approachable. Something people actually want to move toward, rather than "I've got to swallow this pill because I know it's good for me."

KF: On a final, lighter note… What's your favorite DBT skill, and why?

SR: My answer to this has changed as I've gotten older and my life circumstances have shifted. Right now, my favorite is Mindfulness of Current Emotions: fully experiencing whatever I'm feeling, painful or not, without forcing it away or clinging to it. Just letting myself know it's OK to feel whatever I'm feeling, and trusting that it will pass.

JF: That used to be my favorite too, but lately it's Problem Solving. What I've come to appreciate is how much the skill emphasizes specificity. When we encounter something painful, it's easy to make global judgments about ourselves, the situation, or other people. Those global judgments can really keep us stuck in hopelessness, powerlessness, or shame. Problem Solving helps us move from judgments like "I'm a terrible person" toward “This is the specific problem in front of me right now.” It’s much more workable.

KF: Or, “This is my specific problem right now” rather than “The world is a dumpster fire.” I think that’s a good example of why your book feels so perfect for everyone. Life is hard right now, for a lot of people, in a lot of ways. DBT skills offer a concrete way through, and your book makes DBT’s complexity simple and accessible. So thank you for it!
